title-group.article-title: Green and Low-Carbon Urban Renewal Capacity for Sustainable Infrastructure in China: A Spatial Network Analysis

abstract.p: Rapid urbanization concentrates infrastructure demand and places pressure on public services, environmental quality, and resilience. This study assesses provincial capacity to support green and low-carbon urban renewal in China. It examines how this capacity changes and relates to potential interprovincial connections. An index was constructed from 18 indicators across six dimensions for 30 provincial-level regions during 2020–2024. Dimensions received equal weights, with entropy weighting applied within each dimension. The analysis combined kernel-density estimation, spatial autocorrelation, a modified gravity model, social network analysis, and QAP regression. The national mean index increased from 0.222 to 0.360. Global Moran’s I was insignificant in 2020 but significantly positive in 2021–2024. The network of model-derived potential associations was sparse, with distinct incoming, outgoing, and brokerage positions. Urbanization-stage, fiscal-autonomy, and construction-capacity differences, together with geographical adjacency, were positively associated with these modeled ties. Capacity rankings and modeled network positions provide complementary information for identifying relative renewal-capacity shortfalls and screening potential cooperation partners.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Rapid urbanization and continuing rural-to-urban migration have increased demand for urban infrastructure and services. These needs include transport, housing, healthcare, drainage, waste treatment, energy, and digital services. In many rapidly urbanizing regions, urban land expansion and intensification have outpaced infrastructure and public-service provision [1]. Land-development and infrastructure choices can also lock cities into lasting patterns of energy use, spatial organization, and carbon emissions. Reversing these early choices is often difficult and costly [2,3].

Green and low-carbon urban renewal can support infrastructure sustainability by adapting existing land uses and upgrading embedded infrastructure. It improves existing buildings, public facilities, transport systems, environmental infrastructure, public spaces, and governance arrangements. These interventions reduce reliance on outward land expansion and new construction. The scope of sustainable renewal has consequently widened beyond physical redevelopment. It now encompasses environmental performance, economic viability, social inclusion, land-use efficiency, and stakeholder coordination [4,5,6,7].

Three gaps remain in this literature. Infrastructure outcomes are often studied separately. Multidimensional assessments exist for urban sustainability and regeneration [5,6,7]. However, frameworks linking renewal to physical, environmental, social, and digital infrastructure remain limited. Much renewal research also focuses on projects, neighborhoods, or individual cities [4,5,6,8]. Provincial relationships receive less attention. Comparisons of renewal scores also leave open how local response capacity relates to a province’s position in wider networks. Renewal requires locally available resources, while access to external expertise and implementation capacity may matter where those resources are limited.

This study uses a demand–response–coordination framework to link renewal needs, provincial responses, and potential interprovincial connections. Demand concerns mismatches between existing urban stocks and changing service, safety, and environmental requirements. These needs guide indicator selection across six response dimensions. Response encompasses provincial conditions, capacities, and activities supporting green and low-carbon urban renewal. The resulting index enters a modified gravity model to estimate potential interprovincial linkages. Their structure identifies potential connections relevant to coordination. Quadratic Assignment Procedure (QAP) then assesses how provincial differences are associated with the modeled ties. The core question is how provincial capacity for green and low-carbon urban renewal evolved during 2020–2024, and what its potential interprovincial connections imply for renewal planning. The analysis first assesses changes in capacity and its spatial distribution. It then examines network positions and the provincial differences associated with modeled ties. Infrastructure sustainability provides the application context for these findings.

This study extends index-based research on green development and urban sustainability in three ways. First, it incorporates actual renovation starts in old urban residential communities and renewal-related land supply into provincial assessment. These measures add evidence of renewal activity and land support to indicators of broader provincial conditions. Second, DRC explains why adapting existing urban stocks requires both local response capacity and access to resources beyond provincial boundaries. It guides the interpretation of the index and its potential spatial connections. Third, the analysis examines provincial scores, geographical clustering, and directed network positions together. It reveals whether outgoing, incoming, and intermediary roles correspond to provincial renewal capacities. This adds a relational perspective to assessing provincial conditions and identifying potential cooperation opportunities.

sec.title: 2.1. Urban Infrastructure Sustainability Under Rapid Urbanization
sec.p: Infrastructure sustainability and urban resilience are closely related, although their scope differs. Resilience concerns how urban systems resist, absorb, recover from, and adapt to disturbances [9]. Sustainability also considers environmental viability, social inclusion, and economic efficiency over time. This broader perspective treats infrastructure as an interconnected social–ecological–technological system. It helps identify dependencies across sectors and avoid fragmented interventions [10].

Rapid urbanization makes these connections especially relevant. Population growth and spatial redistribution can leave infrastructure demand out of step with service capacity. Infrastructure provision also varies with fiscal capacity, industrial development, technological innovation, governance quality, and environmental constraints. Chinese evidence shows that urbanization can improve some public services while producing uneven regional and sustainability outcomes [11].

sec.title: 2.2. Green and Low-Carbon Urban Renewal as an Infrastructure Sustainability Pathway
sec.p: Urban renewal offers opportunities to improve infrastructure sustainability within existing urban areas. Conventional renewal has often emphasized physical redevelopment, land values, or replacement of deteriorated buildings. Sustainable renewal brings environmental, social, economic, and institutional objectives into planning and implementation [4]. The empirical index assesses provincial conditions and capacities supporting this process. It does not measure completed project outcomes or carbon reductions.

Renovation and adaptive reuse preserve structural materials already present in buildings and infrastructure. They can reduce demand for carbon-intensive construction materials and limit demolition waste. Life-cycle studies show substantial environmental benefits from refurbishment. These assessments consider embodied emissions, operational energy, maintenance, and end-of-life impacts together [12,13]. Retrofit research therefore emphasizes coordination across buildings, infrastructure networks, spatial scales, and resource systems [14]. Green spaces, permeable surfaces, urban forests, and restored waterways can mitigate heat, manage stormwater, improve environmental quality, and support biodiversity. Their contributions to climate mitigation and adaptation extend beyond what carbon indicators capture [15,16]. Integrated optimization studies likewise show benefits from jointly planning green infrastructure, land use, and infrastructure functions [17]. These benefits do not arise automatically. Overlooking distributional effects can increase displacement risks and inequalities in amenity access as environmental redevelopment raises property values [18].

sec.title: 2.3. Spatial Interdependence of Green and Low-Carbon Urban Renewal
sec.p: Spatial interdependence can support diffusion between regions. Network-city theory links complementary advantages and collective benefits to specialization, knowledge exchange, and reciprocal cooperation [19]. Such relationships extend beyond shared geographical borders. Environmental regulation and low-carbon policies may produce spillovers through trade and technological connections. Their effects depend on policy intensity and the structure of interregional relationships [20]. Evidence from China’s dual low-carbon pilot policies shows that coordination can improve urban green land-use efficiency. The associated spillovers can also extend beyond participating cities [21].

Social network analysis represents regions as nodes and their relationships as links. It can therefore examine functional spatial structures beyond administrative contiguity [22]. Studies of interprovincial carbon-emission networks combine gravity models with network analysis. They identify connectivity, central provinces, intermediary regions, and functional blocks that attribute-based analysis alone may miss [23].

sec.title: 2.4. Demand–Response–Coordination Framework
sec.p: The Demand–Response–Coordination (DRC) framework links infrastructure needs, provincial renewal capacity, and potential interregional coordination. Renewal needs guide indicator selection, and the resulting index summarizes provincial response conditions. Uneven access to technology, services, and implementation resources creates a reason to consider coordination beyond local responses. A modified gravity model estimates potential ties among provinces with differing response conditions.

Demand reflects mismatches between existing urban stocks and changing urban requirements. Low-carbon retrofit requires cleaner technologies. Ageing housing and limited service access call for improvements in living conditions. Resource waste and environmental pressures require more efficient and greener urban systems. Safety risks raise requirements for continuity of essential services. Cultural service gaps and heritage protection require stronger cultural and civic provision. Digital service gaps call for better connectivity and governance. Urbanization stage shapes the scale and composition of these needs. These categories identify the reasons for renewal.

Response concerns the conditions and capacities available to address these needs through green and low-carbon renewal. Sustainable renewal integrates economic, environmental, social, technological, and governance objectives with physical reconstruction [4]. To address these renewal needs, provincial response capacity is organized into six dimensions: Innovative, Livable, Beautiful, Resilient, Civilized, and Smart. These dimensions follow the goals set out in China’s Opinions on Promoting High-Quality Urban Development, released in August 20251. These dimensions organize the enabling conditions, renewal activities, and infrastructure provision considered in this study. Their joint assessment draws on research linking infrastructure sustainability to interactions among social, ecological, technological, and institutional systems [10,24,25]. Renewing occupied urban areas requires technical upgrades while essential services continue. Technical resources, service provision, and institutional support therefore need to work together.

Coordination concerns the joint use of resources and experience across provinces to address renewal needs. The modified gravity model uses the renewal index and provincial attributes to estimate potential connections through which such cooperation could develop. These connections indicate structural opportunities, rather than observed cooperation or resource flows. Geographical proximity may facilitate interaction. Organizational, institutional, and cognitive proximity also influence interregional learning and cooperation [26]. Similarity may aid learning, while differences may create complementarity or hinder knowledge absorption. QAP examines these matrix-based associations while accounting for relational dependence [27].

The framework directs attention to three observable aspects of provincial response capacity and its potential connections. Provincial response capacities may cluster spatially, which is examined using Moran’s I. Potential connections may produce unequal centrality and block positions, assessed through network analysis. Urbanization, fiscal, and construction differences may also relate to network ties, examined using QAP. These analyses distinguish the resources available locally from potential connections to resources elsewhere. DRC guides the interpretation of weak response dimensions and the assessment of possible cooperation partners. Figure 1 summarizes these connections. The empirical scope is therefore response capacity and the structural conditions for coordination.

sec.title: 3.1. Conceptual Interpretation and Indicator System
sec.p: Renewal response capacity denotes the provincial resources, service conditions, and institutional support available for upgrading existing urban stocks. The index assesses this capacity in relation to the goal of sustainable infrastructure. It covers economic, social, ecological, institutional, and technological conditions surrounding infrastructure renewal and adaptation. Infrastructure sustainability depends on both facilities and the urban systems in which they operate. These systems shape service access, resource efficiency, environmental quality, adaptation, and long-term governance [2,25,28].

The framework contains six policy-oriented dimensions: Innovative, Livable, Beautiful, Resilient, Civilized, and Smart. Their selection follows the China’s Opinions on Promoting High-Quality Urban Development, released in August 2025. The document was issued by the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the State Council. It identifies these six qualities as the goal for building modern people-centered cities. Each dimension covers a distinct but interdependent aspect of renewal capacity. Together, they describe how renewal can support infrastructure sustainability.

The framework is represented by six dimensions and 18 indicators, with three indicators in each dimension (Table 1). Each dimension receives one-sixth of the total weight. Within each dimension, entropy weights are estimated from all 150 province-year observations. This gives dimensions equal standing while allowing their indicators to differ according to observed variation. Indicator assessments combine information that a single measure cannot capture [5,6,7]. Conceptual relevance was assessed against the needs of adapting existing urban stocks and supporting green and low-carbon renewal. Provincial comparability, non-redundancy, and low correlation also guided indicator selection. The annual number of old urban residential communities where renovation starts measures renewal activity. The share of renewal-related land supply in total land-supply area captures land provision supporting the adaptation of existing urban stocks. The other indicators describe resources and service conditions needed to implement renewal and sustain its use. Their relevance depends on their role in renewal tasks, rather than on general development alone. The supporting indicators cover technological resources, resource-use practices, and conditions for implementing renewal. Valid green and low-carbon technology patents represent relevant technological resources, while reclaimed-water utilization captures water reuse. Service provision, fiscal support, cultural resources, and digital foundations describe complementary conditions for upgrading existing urban areas. Their inclusion reflects the need to maintain essential services, support implementation, and accommodate cultural assets during renewal. Together with renovation starts in old urban residential communities and the renewal-related land-supply share, these indicators assess provincial capacity to support green and low-carbon urban renewal.

The Innovative dimension concerns generating, absorbing, and applying knowledge in urban renewal. Infrastructure transitions require technological experimentation, organizational learning, and cleaner, more efficient production and service models. Urban studies also identify close relationships among innovation, knowledge creation, infrastructure development, and urban growth [29]. The patent indicator counts valid green and low-carbon technology patents. These represent technological resources potentially applicable to cleaner, more resource-efficient renewal. Industrial R&D personnel represent the workforce available to develop and absorb them. Approved national AI innovation and development pilot zones provide institutional platforms that may support innovation in infrastructure management.

The Livable dimension concerns accessible, adequate, safe, and inclusive infrastructure services. Residents’ everyday well-being provides an essential criterion for infrastructure sustainability alongside technical efficiency. The built environment affects mobility, service access, housing conditions, social interaction, environmental experience, and health [30]. Annual renovation starts directly record interventions in old urban residential communities. Counts were compiled from year-end national and provincial housing and urban–rural development disclosures, supplemented by local official releases. The measure captures the scale of renovation activity through actual new starts. Sidewalk provision represents pedestrian service conditions. Renewal-related land supply records land associated with the adaptation of existing stocks, including non-residential uses. The land indicator uses the China Land Transfer Database. It measures renewal-related area as a share of valid recorded land-supply area in each province and year. Records are identified through explicit renewal terms in cleaned project names2. The indicator captures land-supply support for adapting existing stocks.

The Beautiful dimension covers ecological and environmental conditions as well as the visual quality of urban space. Its indicators are reclaimed-water utilization, park green space, and Zero-Waste City policy coverage. Green infrastructure can support ecosystem functions, environmental quality, public health, and well-being simultaneously [31]. Reclaimed-water utilization captures substitution of reused water for additional water demand. Park green space describes ecological and public-space conditions. National Zero-Waste City coverage indicates policy support for waste reduction and resource circulation.

The Resilient dimension concerns maintaining services, withstanding disturbances, recovering from shocks, and adapting to longer-term change [9]. Community health facility density represents decentralized service access. Lower combined-sewer dependence indicates drainage conditions relevant to pollution and stormwater risks. Social security and employment expenditure captures fiscal support for protection and recovery.

The Civilized dimension covers the social, cultural, and institutional foundations of sustainable renewal. Urban social sustainability requires equitable service access and cohesive, viable communities over time [32]. Cultural facilities and social organizations can support place identity, participation, and the social outcomes of regeneration. Assessing these contributions requires multiple indicators beyond economic measures [33]. Library, museum, and sports venue densities form a composite measure of complementary public services. Each density is calculated as the number of facilities divided by population. Social organizations represent participation capacity. Nationally designated historic and cultural towns and villages represent conservation resources and responsibilities.

The Smart dimension concerns digital connectivity, data use, and intelligent governance for coordinating urban systems and improving efficiency. Information and communication technologies can support infrastructure monitoring, integrated services, responsive resource allocation, and informed management. Their contribution to sustainability depends on alignment with environmental and social objectives [34]. Technology is therefore treated as an enabling condition. Smart City pilots and Gigabit City recognition indicate program and connectivity foundations. Digital infrastructure policy attention captures government priorities.

Five indicators measure accumulated designations or policy coverage. The AI pilot-zone indicator counts cumulative approvals, while the heritage indicator counts nationally designated historic towns and villages. The Zero-Waste City, Smart City, and Gigabit City indicators measure the proportion of sampled county-level units covered by these designations. These indicators describe the geographical presence of policy programs and recognized heritage resources relevant to renewal. Annual additions would capture only new designations, excluding those granted before each observation year. Accumulated measures are retained because the assessment concerns provincial renewal conditions rather than the pace of policy designation.

sec.title: 3.2. Data Sources and Data Processing
sec.p: The study covers 30 provincial-level administrative units in China during 2020–2024. Tibet, Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan are excluded because data are unavailable. China’s December 2019 Central Economic Work Conference identified urban renewal and upgrading the existing housing stock as priorities for 2020. Accordingly, 2020 provides a policy-relevant starting point for assessing provincial green and low-carbon urban renewal capacity. The availability and comparability of the selected indicators further restrict the study period to 2020–2024. Sources include provincial statistical series, science and technology statistics, and the China Urban Construction Statistical Yearbook series. Land supply data were obtained from detailed land supply records published on the China Land Market website3. GDP and GDP per capita in the gravity model were converted to 2020 prices using provincial GDP volume indices. Construction output and labor productivity were deflated using provincial industrial producer price indices, also with 2020 as the base. Positive and negative indicators were normalized separately. Combined sewer dependence is negative, while the other 17 indicators are positive. The cultural and sports facility indicator combines three equally weighted density components. Each component is standardized across all 150 observations before aggregation. The composite then enters entropy weighting within its dimension. Sports venue counts cover the retained city sample, while the population denominator is provincial. Normalization and within-dimension entropy estimation use the pooled 150 province-year observations [35]. Higher scores represent a more favorable combination of conditions supporting renewal within this sample.

sec.title: 3.3.1. Entropy Weight TOPSIS Method
sec.p: Entropy weight TOPSIS weights indicators by dispersion and evaluates distances from ideal solutions [35,36]. Let xᵢⱼₜ denote the value of indicator j for province i in year t. Normalization uses all 150 observations for 30 provinces during 2020–2024. Positive and negative indicators are normalized as follows:(1)zijt = (xijt − min xj)/(max xj − min xj)(2)zijt = (max xj − xijt)/(max xj − min xj)

The proportional value, information entropy, information utility, and within-dimension weight of indicator j were calculated as: (3)pijt = zijt/∑i∑tzijt (4)ej=−(1/ln N)∑i∑t(pijtlnpijt) (5)dj=1−ej; ωjwithin=dj∑k∈Jmdk; wj=16ωjwithin

In Equation (5), Jm contains the three indicators in dimension m. The within-dimension weight is ωjwithin, and the final indicator weight is wj. These final weights enter the weighted matrix and distance calculations. N denotes the number of province-year observations. The weighted normalized value is vijt = wjzijt. Distances from the positive and negative ideal solutions are: (6)Dit+ = ∑j(vijt − vj+)2 (7)Dit−=∑j(vijt−vj−)2 where vj+ and vj− denote the maximum and minimum weighted values of indicator j over all 150 province-year observations. The comprehensive score is: (8)Cit = Dit−/(Dit++Dit−)
A larger Cit indicates greater measured capacity for green and low-carbon urban renewal. Each dimension’s score sums its weighted normalized indicators.

sec.title: 3.3.2. Spatial Autocorrelation Analysis
sec.p: Global Moran’s I and Moran scatterplots use a row-standardized economic-geographic weight matrix W [37,38]. The economic-geographic weight matrix combines inverse geographical distance and inverse absolute differences in 2000–2022 mean GDP per capita. Tibet was removed before row standardization, and diagonal entries are zero. Global Moran’s I is: (9)It = (n/S0) ×∑i∑j[wij(Cit−Ct¯)(Cjt−Ct¯)]/∑i(Cit−Ct¯)2 where S0= ∑i∑jwij. Significantly positive values indicate spatial clustering of similar renewal capacities; significantly negative values indicate dispersion. Here, n = 30. Significance uses 9999 permutations and a two-sided comparison of absolute deviations from E(I) = −1/(n − 1). A plus-one correction is applied.

The corresponding local Moran statistic is: (10)Iit = [(Cit−Ct¯)/m2t]∑jwij(Cjt−Ct¯) where m2t= (1/n)∑i(Cit−Ct¯)2. Provinces were classified as High–High, Low–Low, Low–High, or High–Low using their standardized scores and spatially lagged values.

sec.title: 3.3.3. Spatial Association Network Analysis
sec.p: A modified gravity model was used to construct a directed network of potential interprovincial associations based on renewal capacity and provincial attributes: (11)Fijt=Kijt×[GDPitNitCit3×GDPjtNjtCjt3]/[Dij2(git−gjt)2](12)Kijt = Cit/(Cit + Cjt)

GDP denotes real provincial gross domestic product. N denotes the year-end resident population. C denotes the renewal score. g denotes GDP per capita. Dij denotes the geographical distance between provincial capitals. Kijt introduces directionality. Population and GDP represent scale, while the renewal score represents response capacity. Geographical and economic distances represent interaction frictions. Small GDP-per-capita differences can magnify associations, making the network dependent on this specification. The modified gravity model estimates potential interprovincial associations based on renewal capacity and provincial attributes.
Each row’s mean over its 29 off-diagonal values served as the binarization threshold: (13)aijt = 1 if Fijt>Fit¯; otherwise, aijt = 0

Density, connectedness, hierarchy, and efficiency describe the overall network. Density was calculated as:(14)Densityt = Lt/[n(n − 1)] where Lt is the number of modeled directed linkages. In-degree and out-degree measure received and transmitted relationships, respectively. Closeness measures network accessibility, while betweenness identifies provinces in intermediary positions.

CONCOR divided provinces into structurally equivalent blocks. Internal, incoming, and outgoing ties determined their classification as net-spillover, net-beneficiary, broker, or bidirectional-spillover blocks. Block densities were converted to image matrices. An entry equals 1 when its block-to-block density exceeds overall network density, and 0 otherwise. Calculations used UCINET 6.0.

sec.title: 3.3.4. QAP Correlation and Regression Analysis
sec.p: The preceding network analyses describe connectivity patterns and provincial positions. QAP further examines which provincial differences and geographical relationships are associated with the presence of directed network ties. QAP is appropriate because interprovincial relational observations are not statistically independent [27]. The joint model tests whether differences in response conditions are associated with potential links, informing the coordination component of DRC.
The QAP regression model is:(15)Y = β0J + β1URB + β2IND + β3FIS + β4CON + β5EFF + β6ADJ + ε

Y denotes the green and low-carbon urban renewal binary network matrix. URB, IND, FIS, CON, and EFF denote the five difference matrices. ADJ denotes geographical adjacency, and J is the intercept matrix. Six explanatory matrices represent urbanization-stage, industrial-structure, fiscal-autonomy, construction-capacity, and construction-efficiency differences, plus geographical adjacency (Table 2). QAP correlation examines bivariate associations between the dependent and explanatory matrices. QAP regression estimates their joint relationships. A positive coefficient for a continuous difference matrix associates larger provincial differences with the presence of modeled ties. A negative coefficient associates ties with more similar provinces.

sec.title: 4.1. Temporal Evolution of Green and Low-Carbon Urban Renewal Capacity
sec.p: Figure 2 shows the national mean renewal capacity index and weighted dimension scores during 2020–2024. The index rose from 0.222 in 2020 to 0.360 in 2024, an increase of approximately 62.32%. It increased every year, with the largest gain between 2021 and 2022. Annual growth rates nevertheless varied. The dimensions followed different paths. Civilized had the highest mean weighted score in 2020 and 2021. Smart became the largest component from 2022 onward. Beautiful rose from 0.027 to 0.066, with a marked increase in 2022. Smart recorded the largest absolute gain, rising from 0.029 to 0.087 and approximately tripling over the period. Resilient increased from 0.050 to 0.066, while Livable rose from 0.021 to 0.032. Innovative increased from 0.023 to 0.036. Civilized rose from 0.051 in 2020 to 0.052 in 2022 and then declined to 0.048 in 2024.

The overall increase was accompanied by a changing balance among the six dimensions. Smart and Beautiful recorded larger absolute gains, while Civilized lost its initial leading position. These contrasting trajectories indicate that the measured capacities supporting renewal developed at different speeds. A rising composite index can therefore coexist with slower progress or declining scores in individual dimensions.

These differences matter because renewal requires technical upgrades, service continuity, and arrangements for continued use. Faster digital and environmental gains may leave implementation constrained by weaker complementary capacities. The dimensional profile therefore helps identify priorities for closer local assessment, beyond the aggregate trend.

Figure 3 traces changes in the provincial distribution using kernel-density estimates. The curves generally shifted rightward during 2020–2024, showing improvement across provinces alongside the higher national mean. The dominant peak moved from the lower-value range toward the middle, while density at lower capacity values declined. Provincial differences nevertheless persisted. A right-skewed tail and secondary shoulders remained in several years. These features separate the main provincial group from a smaller group with higher scores. Changes in curve height and width also indicate fluctuating dispersion. The distribution moved upward without steadily narrowing or converging into a single tight peak.

sec.title: 4.2. Provincial Distribution and Regional Differences
sec.p: Figure 4 compares the spatial distribution in 2020 and 2024 using common classification intervals. Scores generally moved into higher categories, although differences persisted. Zhejiang ranked highest in 2020 (0.389) and 2024 (0.550). Other high-scoring provinces in 2024 included Tianjin (0.533), Beijing (0.479), Jiangsu (0.468), Shanghai (0.441), and Shandong (0.432).

All 30 provinces had higher index values in 2024 than in 2020, although their trajectories differed (Figure 5). Zhejiang rose from 0.389 to 0.550, and Tianjin from 0.235 to 0.533. Beijing increased from 0.346 to 0.479. Jiangsu rose from 0.240 to 0.468, while Shanghai increased from 0.230 to 0.441. Beijing ranked first in 2021; Zhejiang led in the other four years.

Several central and western provinces also recorded substantial gains. Hubei rose from 0.213 to 0.395, and Jiangxi from 0.193 to 0.402. Henan increased from 0.174 to 0.358. Sichuan rose from 0.200 to 0.350, while Guizhou increased from 0.166 to 0.308. Improvement therefore extended beyond the eastern coast.

Lower scores in 2024 occurred in Yunnan (0.203), Gansu (0.241), Hainan (0.251), Hunan (0.261), and Xinjiang (0.262). Higher scores were concentrated in the east, although provincial differences did not follow a strict east–central–west ordering. Earlier provincial research similarly identifies persistent heterogeneity in green development [39].

Provinces with the highest scores did not necessarily record the largest gains. Tianjin’s increase exceeded Zhejiang’s despite its lower initial score. Substantial gains in several central and western provinces also show that progress extended beyond the eastern concentration of high scores. The spatial pattern therefore combines widespread improvement with persistent differences in provincial standing. Renewal conditions remain uneven, but their evolution does not follow a uniform regional sequence.

For planning, initial capacity and subsequent improvement answer different questions. The former indicates available conditions; the latter shows how those conditions have changed. A rapidly improving province may still require external support, while a high-scoring province may have weaknesses in individual dimensions. Provincial rankings should therefore be read alongside dimensional profiles and local renewal requirements.

sec.title: 4.3. Spatial Autocorrelation and Moran Scatterplots
sec.p: Table 3 reports Global Moran’s I during 2020–2024. The 2020 coefficient was positive but insignificant. Coefficients were positive and significant at 1% in 2021–2024. Similar provincial scores were therefore spatially associated under the specified economic-geographic matrix in those years. Moran’s I rose to 0.349 in 2021 and declined to 0.271 in 2022. It then increased to 0.291 in 2023 and 0.306 in 2024. Spatial association fluctuated, without a continuous weakening trend.

Figure 6 plots standardized provincial scores against their spatial lags. High–High counts were 8, 6, 6, 9, and 8 provinces during 2020–2024, respectively. These provinces had above-average scores and positive spatial lags. Low–Low counts were 13, 18, 12, 12, and 12, respectively. Low–High and High–Low observations also occurred. Provincial scores and surrounding weighted values therefore did not always have the same sign.

Low–Low observations outnumber High–High observations in every year, indicating that the below-average configuration is more prevalent in the sample. Mixed-quadrant observations show that some provincial scores differ from the pattern represented by their weighted spatial surroundings. The significant global spatial association during 2021–2024 therefore coexists with heterogeneous provincial positions. This pattern is consistent with shared regional conditions, but does not by itself distinguish common influences from interprovincial transmission.

The largest annual index increase coincided with a decline in Moran’s I between 2021 and 2022. Aggregate improvement therefore did not imply stronger spatial clustering. Where below-average conditions occur together, nearby provinces may face similar resource constraints. This provides a reason to examine potential connections beyond the immediate spatial pattern.

sec.title: 4.4.1. Overall Network Structure
sec.p: Table 4 summarizes the directed association network. Connectedness remained 1 throughout 2020–2024. Several provinces nevertheless had zero in-degree, so this value does not imply mutual reachability for every ordered pair. Density varied within a narrow range. It rose from 0.197 in 2020 to 0.205 in 2021 and 0.208 in 2022. It fell to 0.207 in 2023 before reaching 0.210 in 2024. About one-fifth of all possible directed provincial ties were present. Hierarchy ranged from 0.515 to 0.554. It remained at 0.554 in 2020–2021, fell to 0.515 in 2022, and returned to 0.552 in 2023–2024. The network retained a hierarchical structure, with little difference between the endpoints. Network efficiency here reflects structural redundancy; its endpoint decline suggests more alternative paths. Overall, substantial capacity growth coincided with persistently low density and little change in endpoint hierarchy. Provincial improvement was therefore more pronounced than changes in the distribution of modeled connections. This uneven structure accords with provincial green-infrastructure and regional eco-efficiency studies identifying differentiated networks extending beyond geographical adjacency [40,41]. Because ties are defined relative to each row mean, these changes describe network structure rather than cooperation volume. The contrast between rising capacity and relatively stable connectivity makes provincial network positions important: aggregate growth alone does not reveal where connections concentrate or which provinces link them.

sec.title: 4.4.2. Provincial Network Positions
sec.p: Figure 7 compares provincial centrality in 2020 and 2024 with paired markers. Movement rightward indicates an increase, while movement leftward indicates a decrease. High outgoing connectivity was not confined to provinces with the highest index scores. Guangdong, Guangxi, Guizhou, and Gansu shared the highest normalized out-degree in 2024: 31.034, corresponding to nine outgoing ties. Guangdong, Chongqing, Guangxi, and Guizhou each had eight outgoing ties in 2020 (27.586).

Incoming ties describe the direction of modeled associations. Shanghai led in-degree in both years at 89.655, equivalent to 26 incoming ties. Beijing and Jiangsu followed at 86.207 (25 ties). Zhejiang had 18 incoming ties (62.069) in both years. Qinghai, Xinjiang, Shaanxi, and Heilongjiang were among the provinces with no incoming ties in 2024.

Beijing (87.879), Shanghai (85.294), and Jiangsu (82.857) had the highest in-closeness in 2024. Out-closeness was highest in Xinjiang (9.539), Heilongjiang (9.091), and Gansu (8.815). Some ordered province pairs were unreachable in this directed network.

Beijing had the highest betweenness in both years, rising from 13.887 to 14.221. Henan increased from 9.451 to 11.184. Fujian declined from 9.491 to 6.630, while Jiangxi fell from 8.397 to 6.005. These provinces held prominent intermediary positions in 2024.

The centrality patterns reveal a stable incoming core alongside a changing intermediary structure. Shanghai, Beijing, and Jiangsu retain prominent incoming positions, while outgoing connectivity is more geographically dispersed. These roles do not follow capacity rankings: Gansu combines high out-degree with a relatively low capacity score. Beijing remained the main intermediary, while Henan’s strengthening brokerage suggests a connecting role not captured by capacity rankings. Declining betweenness in Fujian and Jiangxi also shows that intermediary positions can change. Network analysis thus complements capacity assessment by distinguishing where modeled ties converge, originate, and pass through intermediaries. Potential cooperation partners should be assessed through both their relevant resources and their network positions.

sec.title: 4.4.3. Block Structure and Inter-Block Relationships
sec.p: CONCOR identified four blocks in each endpoint year (Table 5). In 2020, Blocks 1 and 2 were net-spillover blocks; Blocks 3 and 4 were net-beneficiary blocks. In 2024, Block 1 remained net spillover and Block 3 remained net beneficiary. Block 2 became bidirectional spillover, and Block 4 became a broker. These labels reflect the balance and internal share of modeled ties.

Block 1’s internal ties fell from seven to five, and its internal-relation ratio declined from 7.69% to 4.90%. Its outgoing external ties increased from 84 to 97. Block 2’s internal ties rose from three to ten, with its internal ratio increasing from 6.98% to 34.48%. Block 3’s incoming external ties rose from 32 to 88. Block 4’s internal ties fell from eight to one.

Table 6 shows two image entries changing from zero to one: Block 2’s internal entry and Block 4 to Block 3. Block 2 to Block 4 and Block 4’s internal entry changed from one to zero. Block 4 to Block 1 remained one, with 19 directed ties in each year.

Figure 8 traces changes in block membership. Hubei moved from Block 1 to Block 4, and Chongqing from Block 2 to Block 4. Jilin and Ningxia moved from Block 2 to Block 1. Tianjin moved from Block 3 to Block 2. Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang moved from Block 4 to Block 3. Ribbons indicate membership changes, while arrows show inter-block ties within each year. Figure 8 also summarizes inter-block tie counts. Block 1 to Block 3 increased from 15 to 60, while Block 1 to Block 4 declined from 65 to 34. Block 2 to Block 4 fell from 19 to zero, and Block 4 to Block 3 rose from one to ten.

Figure 9 shows the endpoint networks. Nodes represent provinces, and arrows indicate gravity values above the corresponding row mean. Shanghai, Beijing, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang retained prominent incoming connectivity. Other provinces occupied outgoing or intermediary positions.

The block patterns suggest a reorganization of potential connections rather than uniformly stronger integration. The expanding Block 1–Block 3 channel indicates greater concentration toward incoming hubs, while Block 2 developed stronger internal cohesion. Block 4’s brokerage despite weak internal connectivity shows that intermediary importance can depend on connections between groups. Greater connectivity therefore does not necessarily mean more balanced participation or stronger cohesion across the network. Membership changes also matter: Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang’s movement into Block 3 contributes to its increased incoming connectivity. The endpoint differences thus reflect both provincial regrouping and changes in ties. These patterns provide a basis for screening potential partners within and across blocks, with attention to shared renewal needs, relevant expertise, and construction resources. Planning should therefore assess specific tasks and partner capabilities, rather than assign permanent functions to the identified blocks.

sec.title: 4.5. Factors Associated with Interprovincial Network Ties
4.5.1. QAP Correlation Results
sec.p: Table 7 reports QAP correlations between the binary network and the six explanatory matrices. All absolute correlation coefficients are below 0.500, indicating modest bivariate associations. Urbanization-stage differences show the largest coefficients, ranging from 0.361 to 0.403 across the three comparisons. Multicollinearity among the explanatory matrices was assessed separately using VIF diagnostics (Appendix A, Table A1). All VIF values are below 2.000 in the 2020, 2024, and average-input models, indicating no serious multicollinearity.

sec.title: 4.5.2. QAP Regression Results
sec.p: Table 8 identifies associations between network ties and differences in provincial conditions relevant to renewal demand and implementation. Urbanization-stage differences have the largest standardized coefficients (0.285–0.328) across the three models. These differences may capture varying combinations of housing renovation, land redevelopment, and public-service upgrading needs. This interpretation reflects urban renewal’s focus on adapting existing urban stocks to changing requirements. Positive fiscal-autonomy and construction-capacity coefficients are consistent with potential complementarity between renewal demands and implementation resources. Renewal projects require financing and construction capabilities to coordinate retrofit, infrastructure replacement, and continued service provision.

Industrial-structure differences show weaker and less consistent associations. Urban renewal spans residential, industrial, and public-service assets, so industrial composition may capture only part of its requirements. Construction-efficiency differences are insignificant in the main models. Aggregate construction labor productivity may not fully capture the specialized capabilities required for retrofit and work within existing urban areas. The results therefore suggest that modeled renewal linkages are associated with selected differences in needs and resources, alongside geographical proximity.

These associations suggest that renewal connections involve differences in needs and implementation resources. Provinces at different urbanization stages face different combinations of housing adaptation, service upgrading, and infrastructure replacement. Their positive association with network ties suggests that potential connections extend across these different renewal contexts. Fiscal-autonomy differences concern the financing conditions under which such needs can be addressed. Unlike new development, renewal often involves existing residents, fragmented property rights, and public facilities with limited direct financial returns. These features make funding commitments and the allocation of costs central to implementation. Construction-capacity differences, in turn, concern the resources available to undertake physical adaptation. Their positive association suggests that potential connections may link differing renewal requirements with unequal construction resources.

Construction-efficiency differences were insignificant, indicating that productivity gaps alone do not explain ties once the other conditions are considered. Renewal requires more than efficient construction: projects must accommodate existing uses, coordinate participants, and maintain essential services. The positive adjacency association is consistent with the practical value of proximity for site coordination and repeated interaction. Together, these findings suggest that cooperation should begin with specific renewal tasks and the resources needed to complete them. Differences identify possible grounds for cooperation, while their practical value depends on whether provincial resources fit those tasks.

Robustness tests use 2000 and 10,000 permutations, and a threshold of 1.1 times the row mean (Appendix A, Table A3, Table A4 and Table A5). Urbanization-stage, fiscal-autonomy, and construction-capacity differences retain positive, significant coefficients, as does geographical adjacency. Construction efficiency remains insignificant. One-year-lagged QAP regressions address potential endogeneity, with results broadly consistent with those in Table 8 (Appendix A, Table A2).

sec.title: 5.1. Capacity Composition and the Implementation of Renewal
sec.p: The principal temporal finding is a change in the composition of renewal capacity alongside its overall growth. Environmental and digital components expanded more rapidly, while innovation grew more slowly and the sociocultural component declined after 2022. Infrastructure research emphasizes interdependence among technological, ecological, and social systems [2,10,28]. This perspective highlights the complementary capacities needed to implement renewal. Digital monitoring still requires staff able to act on information. Resource-reuse facilities require maintenance and compatible service networks. Retrofitting occupied neighborhoods also requires continuity of essential services and arrangements that residents can use [9,42]. A gain in one component cannot necessarily compensate for a weakness elsewhere.

The green and low-carbon orientation is particularly relevant to this conversion from available resources to practical use. Valid green and low-carbon technology patents represent a technological resource, while reclaimed-water utilization records an operating reuse practice. Wider digital and environmental foundations may help apply such resources, but suitable procurement, adaptation, and maintenance are still needed. Research on smart sustainability similarly identifies tensions between technological expansion and inclusive, environmentally effective use [34,43]. The smaller Innovative gain alongside rapid Smart growth therefore directs attention to applying relevant technologies, rather than treating digital coverage as a substitute for technical capability.

The Civilized trajectory raises a related question about the social conditions that sustain renewal. Cultural facilities, social organizations, and heritage resources support different aspects of public life [29,32]. Zheng et al.’s Xinhua Community study links participatory renewal to recurring activities, organizational support, and the gradual distribution of coordination roles [44]. Cultural and heritage resources require continuing investment, communication, and planning feedback to support their conservation and adaptation [45]. Their contribution to renewal therefore depends on how they are maintained and connected to residents’ needs. The uneven dimensional trends therefore warrant attention to how existing resources are maintained and used, alongside investment in new facilities.

sec.title: 5.2. Provincial Differences and the Scope for Resource Matching
sec.p: The spatial findings show that general improvement has not removed differences in the capacity available for renewal. Higher-scoring eastern provinces coexist with substantial gains elsewhere, while positive Moran statistics indicate clustering during 2021–2024. Similarity in the spatial distribution and differences associated with network ties are not contradictory. The former describes where comparable conditions occur; the latter identifies provincial pairs linked under the gravity specification. Together they suggest examining both shared regional constraints and connections to provinces with different resources. Urban energy research also shows that effective interventions vary with development stage and urban conditions [46]. A common renewal objective therefore need not imply a common intervention package.

The QAP findings narrow the conditions relevant to this matching process. Urbanization-stage differences are associated with ties alongside fiscal and construction-capacity differences. In existing urban areas, implementation must reconcile adaptation needs with funding and delivery resources. Research on local public expenditure supports the relevance of fiscal arrangements to infrastructure provision [47,48]. A plausible interpretation is that differing implementation contexts create reasons to seek expertise or resources elsewhere. Yet differences are useful only when a specific resource answers a specific need. The policy implication is to test such matches, rather than assume that any pair with different provincial conditions is complementary.

Adjacency’s positive association adds a practical consideration: cross-border arrangements may be easier to sustain where participants can interact repeatedly. Proximity research nevertheless distinguishes geographical proximity from organizational and institutional compatibility [26]. External knowledge also requires local expertise able to recognize and apply it [49]. For example, technical assistance for reclaimed-water systems would require local operation and maintenance capability as well as an experienced partner. Provinces with weaker capacities may therefore need support for receiving and using assistance, alongside access to external resources.

sec.title: 5.3. Network Positions and Potential Partner Screening
sec.p: The network findings distinguish access to potential partners from the capacity to organize cooperation. A stable incoming core coexists with changing intermediary positions and uneven cohesion within blocks. These configurations resemble the differentiated structures reported in other regional environmental networks [40,41]. However, the present results also show why a single ranking of provinces is insufficient. Gansu’s high out-degree does not make it the leading source of renewal resources. Henan’s intermediary position identifies a different possibility from the high capacity scores of several coastal provinces. The relevant question is whether a province’s expertise and organizational capacity warrant its inclusion among potential partners.

Cooperation requires organizations that can assemble resources while maintaining participation among the actors responsible for implementation. Chinese urban renewal studies show that concentrated coordination can simplify decisions but also increase dependence on a central organization [50]. Sustained participation and shared organizational roles offer complementary ways to maintain collaboration [44]. These findings suggest assessing organizational capacity and existing working relationships when screening provinces with intermediary positions as potential partners.

The block findings identify different patterns of potential association. Block 2’s greater internal cohesion contrasts with Block 4’s position linking groups. These patterns can inform an initial search for potential partners within and across blocks. Inclusion in a shortlist should depend on relevant expertise and compatibility with identified renewal needs, rather than centrality or block membership alone.

sec.title: 5.4. Implications for Renewal Planning and Partner Screening
sec.p: Planning can use the findings through a sequence that starts with local requirements and then examines external support. The provincial dimensions identify areas for closer diagnosis, while the direct renewal indicators locate activity involving old residential communities and existing land. City and project assessments should then specify the relevant service gaps, environmental requirements, and operational constraints. Land redevelopment and housing renovation can be coordinated with drainage, community services, and resource-reuse facilities where these assessments demonstrate a need. This approach accords with research linking ecological management to integrated blue–green and gray infrastructure planning [16,31,51]. Local assessment remains necessary across provinces with different capacity scores.

Potential partner screening should follow the identification of specific renewal shortfalls. The QAP associations justify examining differences in financial and construction resources, alongside proximity. Network positions can inform an initial shortlist, while relevant expertise and compatibility with local renewal needs provide criteria for further assessment. A lower-capacity province seeking retrofit support might prioritize an experienced technical team and compatible delivery arrangements over a partner’s overall rank.

sec.title: 5.5. Theoretical Contributions and Limitations
sec.p: The combined findings distinguish improving response conditions from organizing their use across provinces. Capacity rose substantially, yet network density changed little and provincial roles remained unequal. Within DRC, this means that a stronger response does not itself demonstrate stronger coordination. The theoretical implication is to consider both the composition of local capacity and the relationships through which it could be applied. Research on regional absorptive capacity and urban renewal governance suggests that local expertise and sustained organizational relationships help put available resources into practice [44,49,50]. Within DRC, this perspective directs attention to where local resources are insufficient, whether external resources fit the task, and how cooperation could sustain their use.

This interpretation also sets the scope of the theoretical argument. The gravity network partly derives from the capacity index, and QAP examines associations within that modeled structure. It does not independently test resource exchange or the organizational mechanisms identified in project studies. Further research could test the proposed matching process using observed agreements, technical assistance, construction-service provision, and project outcomes. Combining these records with city-level assessments would also help establish whether stronger response capacity improves service continuity and environmental performance.

The short study period includes the COVID-19 pandemic and associated policy responses. Facility stocks and established policy coverage are less directly sensitive to temporary lockdowns than attendance or economic activity. Nevertheless, renovation starts and land supply may have shifted between years through delays. Social security and employment expenditure may reflect relief measures, while construction output may reflect disruption and policy support. The 2021–2022 increase therefore cannot be attributed solely to sustained capacity improvement. Cumulative designations also capture established coverage rather than verified implementation gains. These measurement limits affect the interpretation of annual changes, even where the broad pattern survives alternative specifications.

sec.title: 6. Conclusions
sec.p: Provincial green and low-carbon urban renewal capacity increased during 2020–2024, but its composition and potential interprovincial connections remained uneven. The analysis yields three main conclusions.

First, the mean index rose from 0.222 to 0.360, with gains in all 30 provinces. Smart and Beautiful expanded faster, while Civilized declined after 2022. Spatial association was significantly positive during 2021–2024. Overall improvement therefore coexisted with dimensional and geographical differences.

Second, the density of the potential association network increased slightly, from 0.197 to 0.210. Within this modeled network, a stable incoming core coexisted with changing intermediary positions and uneven internal cohesion. Capacity rankings and network roles provided different information about provincial resources and potential connections.

Third, urbanization-stage, fiscal-autonomy, and construction-capacity differences, together with adjacency, were positively associated with model-derived potential ties. These associations persisted across the reported robustness checks. Industrial structure was less consistently significant, and construction-efficiency differences were insignificant.

The findings support identifying relative shortfalls across renewal-capacity dimensions and screening potential cooperation partners. Within DRC, capacity assessment identifies areas requiring closer local diagnosis, while potential associations inform an initial search for relevant external expertise.
